screens.title: Introduction to Ansible for Configuration Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we build a practical foundation for using Ansible to automate configuration across many servers. You will learn the core architecture — control node, managed nodes, and the inventory — and how Ansible’s agentless model uses SSH to keep setup simple and secure. We will walk through ad-hoc commands for quick checks, then develop a simple playbook that installs and manages Nginx, showing conditionals for different Linux families. You’ll see how modules and tasks produce idempotent changes, why that matters in production, and common mistakes to avoid when configuring inventories and privilege escalation. Finally, you will get a short hands-on lab to create a user and a shared project directory, reinforcing the workflow from inventory to playbook execution. By the end you should be able to run simple ad-hoc commands, author basic playbooks, and reason about when to test versus apply changes in a live environment. Consider how automation reduces manual error and think about which repetitive tasks you would automate first.

keyIdea.text: Ansible is an agentless automation engine that uses a control node, an inventory, and idempotent modules to reliably manage system state across many servers over SSH.

content.html:
Module 09 › Chapter 9.4 › Introduction to Ansible
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Ansible fundamentals for configuration management
Estimated time: 12–18 minutes

Introduction to Ansible

A hands-on introduction to agentless automation, inventories, modules, ad-hoc commands, and playbooks to manage system state consistently.

In this lesson
Control node and managed nodes, inventory and groups, ad-hoc commands, writing a simple Nginx playbook, and a lab to create a user and directory.
Why it matters
Automation reduces manual errors and scales configuration across dozens or hundreds of servers while preserving reproducibility and auditability.
Key takeaway
Agentless SSH and idempotent modules let you describe desired state and apply it reliably across diverse systems.
Visual summary
Control node drives managed nodes using an inventory and modules over SSH.
Control Node
Your workstation or server with Ansible and Python installed. Runs playbooks and ad-hoc commands.
Managed Nodes
Target servers reachable via SSH. No Ansible agent required; standard OS tooling and Python are used.
Inventory
A hosts file or dynamic source that organizes servers into groups and allows variables per host or group.
Playbook
YAML file that maps hosts to tasks, using modules to perform idempotent operations and manage desired state.
Explore Key Topics
Inventory & Groups
Organize hosts so plays target the right machines.
Modules & Idempotence
Modules make changes predictable when rerun.
Playbooks & Testing
YAML plays with conditionals and become for privilege escalation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives map to tangible skills you will practice. First, you will explain Ansible’s core concepts and architecture so you can reason about why agentless SSH is both simple and secure; understanding this avoids the common trap of assuming an agent is required. Second, you will set up a control node and configure managed nodes for reliable communication, including SSH key setup and inventory placement. Third, you will run ad-hoc commands to perform immediate checks and fixes; this helps you validate connectivity and run quick diagnostics without writing a playbook. Fourth, you will author simple playbooks to perform repeatable configuration tasks, like installing packages and managing services, and use become and when conditionals to keep tasks safe across distributions. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint to help remember the workflow from inventory to execution. These objectives are intentionally hands-on so you practice both quick commands and structured, reusable automation.

screens.title: Why Configuration Management matters and Ansible’s role
screens.narratorSegment: Configuration Management exists because hand-editing dozens of machines is error-prone and slow. When each host drifts from the documented state, debugging grows harder and outages become likely. Ansible addresses that by letting you express desired state and apply it consistently. A core claim is that automation should be readable, version-controlled, and repeatable. Ansible’s strengths are its agentless architecture and its module library. Being agentless means targets need only standard SSH and, usually, Python. That reduces deployment overhead and easing security reviews. Idempotence is another key idea: modules should make the same change only once and leave the system in the desired state on subsequent runs. For example, using the apt module with state: present installs a package only if it’s missing; running the same task again will not reinstall. A common misconception is that automation removes human oversight; in reality, it shifts your role to designing correct state and tests. To practice, pick one repetitive task you perform today and imagine expressing it as an idempotent Ansible task. What would you need to check first? Why Configuration Management matters and Ansible’s role means configuration management expresses desired state so systems converge predictably and repeatedly; ansible implements this with agentless ssh and idempotent modules.. In practical terms, managing state, reducing error, and scaling changes reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Configuration Management expresses desired state so systems converge predictably and repeatedly; Ansible implements this with agentless SSH and idempotent modules.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why CM and Ansible

Ansible helps you declare the desired state of systems, making changes repeatable and auditable. Its agentless model and idempotent modules reduce overhead and unintended side effects.

Key Benefit
Fewer manual edits, lower drift, faster recovery.
Common Misconception
Automation eliminates humans — false. It amplifies design and review responsibilities.
Example
Using apt with state: present ensures a package is installed once and not reinstalled on subsequent runs, preserving idempotence.
Illustration: state-driven change
A task expresses desired result rather than raw commands.
Imperative
Run raw shell commands to install a package each time; risk duplicates and errors.
Declarative (Ansible)
Define package with state: present; Ansible ensures desired state and leaves system unchanged if already compliant.
Practical check
  • Identify a repetitive task you do today.
  • Express it as an idempotent goal: ensure package, file, or service state.
  • Test with an ad-hoc command then write a playbook to automate it.
Key Takeaway

Design automation around desired state and idempotent modules to reduce drift and enable safe, repeatable changes.

screens.title: Ansible architecture: Control node, managed nodes, and SSH
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding Ansible architecture helps you design where automation runs and how credentials are managed. The control node is the machine that runs ansible or ansible-playbook; it needs Python and the Ansible package. Managed nodes are the hosts listed in your inventory and do not require an agent because Ansible connects over SSH. When you execute a play, Ansible pushes a small module payload to the managed node and runs it remotely. That module performs the requested operation and returns structured results. This flow means SSH connectivity, key management, and host reachability are critical dependencies. A concrete example: running ansible webservers -m ping from the control node opens SSH connections to each host in the webservers group and executes a small python-based ping module that returns success or failure. A common misconception is that modules remain installed on managed nodes; they are transferred temporarily and removed after execution. Key takeaway: secure SSH keys and verify inventory reachability before automating large runs. How would you validate reachability in your environment? Ansible architecture: Control node, managed nodes, and SSH means control node runs playbooks and pushes temporary modules over ssh to managed nodes, which execute and return results—no persistent agent required.. In practical terms, how communication and execution flow in an agentless model. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Architecture Summary
keyIdea.text: Control node runs playbooks and pushes temporary modules over SSH to managed nodes, which execute and return results—no persistent agent required.

content.html:
Definition

Parts of the architecture

  • Control node: Runs Ansible CLI and playbooks; requires Python and Ansible.
  • Inventory: Hosts file or dynamic source that groups managed nodes.
  • Managed nodes: Targets reachable via SSH; modules execute briefly and return results.
  • Communication: SSH with keys is recommended for secure, passwordless operation.
Misconception
Ansible installs an agent — false. Modules are copied and run momentarily; no persistent agent is required.
Execution flow
1. Command
You run ansible or ansible-playbook from control node.
2. Push module
Ansible copies a module payload to managed nodes over SSH.
3. Execute & return
The module runs and returns a result to the control node for reporting.
Concrete example
Running ansible webservers -m ping connects to each host in the webservers group, executes a small ping module, and reports success or failure back to the control node.
Key Takeaway

Secure SSH and inventory validation are prerequisites for reliable automation; modules are ephemeral and do not leave agents behind.

screens.title: Inventory basics: groups, host vars, and formats
screens.narratorSegment: An inventory is simply a list of managed nodes organized into groups. The simplest inventory is an INI-style file, often at /etc/ansible/hosts or a custom file you pass with -i. Groups let you target logical sets like webservers or databases. You can also assign variables per-host or per-group to control behavior. For example, adding web1. example. com ansible_user=devops next to a host sets a connection user for that host. Dynamic inventories are scripts or plugins that pull hosts from cloud providers; they are useful when hosts change frequently. A practical example: create a hosts file with a webservers group and a databases group, then run ansible webservers -m ping to verify reachability. Common mistakes include malformed INI syntax or forgetting to expose SSH keys for the user specified in ansible_user. When building inventories, keep them simple and test group targets with the ping module before running playbooks. Which groups would you create for your own infrastructure and why? Inventory basics: groups, host vars, and formats means inventories group hosts and can define per-host or per-group variables; always test groups and connection variables before running playbooks.. In practical terms, organize hosts so plays target the correct machines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Inventories group hosts and can define per-host or per-group variables; always test groups and connection variables before running playbooks.

content.html:
Process Flow

Inventory structure

Use groups and optional variables to target hosts precisely. Keep files readable and versioned with your config repo.

Example hosts file
[webservers]
web1.example.com
web2.example.com

[databases]
db1.example.com ansible_user=dbadmin
Tips
  • Version your inventory or generate it dynamically for cloud environments.
  • Set ansible_user when the SSH login differs from your control node user.
  • Test groups with ansible -m ping before running changes.

Common mistakes

Formatting errors
Missing newlines or incorrect spacing can make hosts invisible to Ansible.
Wrong connection user
If ansible_user is wrong, SSH will fail; prefer key-based authentication and test with ping.
Dynamic inventories
When hosts change often, use dynamic sources but validate the output format matches Ansible expectations.
Key Takeaway

Group hosts logically, set connection vars explicitly when needed, and always verify reachability before applying playbooks.

screens.title: Modules and idempotence
screens.narratorSegment: Modules are the building blocks of Ansible tasks. Each module encapsulates a specific administrative action — install a package, manage a service, copy a file, or manage users. A crucial property of good modules is idempotence: executing the module multiple times should leave the system in the same state as running it once. Consider the apt module with state: present. If a package is already installed, the module should report no change and not reinstall. This behavior is what lets you run playbooks repeatedly for drift correction without fear of repeated side effects. Modules are executed remotely: Ansible copies the module to the managed node, runs it, and interprets the result. A common mistake is using the shell module for tasks that have a native module; shell commands are often non-idempotent and harder to test. For example, prefer ansible. builtin. user to create a system user rather than a shell adduser sequence. As a practice, review tasks and ask: is there a module that does this idempotently? If so, use it. How might a non-idempotent shell task cause problems when rerun?

keyIdea.title: Modules matter
keyIdea.text: Choose idempotent modules over raw shell commands to make playbooks predictable and safe to rerun.

content.html:
Core Concept

What modules do

Modules perform discrete tasks and return structured results. They are transferred and executed remotely and should aim to be idempotent.

Popular modules
  • ansible.builtin.apt / yum / package — manage packages
  • ansible.builtin.service — manage services
  • ansible.builtin.copy / file — manage files and permissions
  • ansible.builtin.user / group — manage accounts
Misuse
Using shell when a module exists makes tasks non-idempotent and brittle across distributions.

Concrete example

Idempotent: 
- name: Ensure nginx installed
  ansible.builtin.apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present
Non-idempotent shell: 
- name: Install nginx with shell
  ansible.builtin.shell: |
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx
Key Takeaway

Prefer native modules for predictable, repeatable results. Reserve shell for tasks without module support and test carefully.

screens.title: Write your first playbook — install_nginx.yml
screens.narratorSegment: Playbooks are YAML files that map groups of hosts to a set of tasks. This example configures Nginx across webservers, handling Debian and RedHat families defensively. The play begins with a name and hosts, then sets become: true so installation and service management run with elevated privileges. Tasks call fully qualified modules like ansible. builtin. apt and ansible. builtin. yum depending on ansible_os_family. The when conditional uses facts gathered by Ansible to target package manager-specific steps. Running ansible-playbook -i hosts install_nginx. yml executes the play across the specified inventory. A common misconception is that when conditions slow runs — they are a safe way to prevent errors by avoiding inappropriate module calls. Example: if a Debian host runs the apt task the package is installed; a RedHat host will skip that task and run the yum task instead. Practice: try a dry run with --check to confirm what will change before applying. What would you add to make the play more robust for custom package names or versions? In practical terms, a cross-distribution playbook using when conditionals and become. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. keyIdea.title: Playbook pattern
keyIdea.text: Playbooks express multi-host workflows; use become for privileged tasks and when conditions to handle OS differences safely.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
install_nginx.yml
---
- name: Configure Nginx web servers
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure Nginx package is installed
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        name: nginx
        state: present
      when: ansible_os_family == "Debian"

    - name: Ensure Nginx package is installed (RedHat)
      ansible.builtin.yum:
        name: nginx
        state: present
      when: ansible_os_family == "RedHat"

    - name: Ensure Nginx service is running and enabled at boot
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true
Explaining the blocks
  • hosts: targets the webservers group from inventory.
  • become: escalates privileges for tasks requiring root.
  • when: conditional guards tasks by OS family facts.
  • modules: apt, yum, and service ensure idempotent operations.
Key Takeaway

Structure plays for clarity: name the play, set hosts and become, then list idempotent tasks with conditionals when required.

screens.title: Ad-hoc commands: quick checks and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Ad-hoc commands are one-off Ansible invocations used for quick diagnostics or immediate fixes without creating a playbook. They are useful for validation steps like connectivity checks or fast changes when a scripted playbook would be overkill. A typical example is ansible all -m ping which runs the ping module across every host in the inventory and returns success or failure. Another common ad-hoc usage is ansible webservers -a "uptime" which runs a simple command using the default command module. For package operations you can call a module directly: ansible databases -m apt -a "name=postgresql state=present" to ensure a package is installed on a database group. Remember that ad-hoc commands are powerful but not version-controlled; for repeatable configurations prefer playbooks. A common pitfall is using ad-hoc commands for complex sequences; if you need repeatability or testing, convert the sequence to a playbook. screens.title: Set up a control node and configure managed nodes
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up a control node and managed nodes is a deliberate sequence of steps. First, install Ansible on your control node using your distribution package manager. On Debian: update and apt install ansible; on RHEL-family use dnf or yum. Second, generate SSH keys on the control node with ssh-keygen and copy the public key to managed nodes using ssh-copy-id or manual authorized_keys editing. This enables passwordless authentication, which Ansible prefers. Third, create an inventory file named hosts or my_inventory and add your target hosts into logical groups. Optionally set ansible_user per host if different from your control node account. Fourth, test connectivity with ansible all -m ping or ansible -m ping to confirm reachability. A common mistake is forgetting to configure Python on older minimal images; ensure Python is present as many modules rely on it. Finally, version your inventory and any connection variables in your automation repository so others can reproduce your setup. After these steps you can run ad-hoc commands and playbooks safely. content.html:
Lab Walkthrough
setup_dev_environment.yml
---
- name: Setup development user and project directory
  hosts: target_servers
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure 'devuser' group exists
      ansible.builtin.group:
        name: devuser
        state: present

    - name: Ensure 'devuser' user exists with home directory
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: devuser
        group: devuser
        shell: /bin/bash
        state: present
        create_home: true

    - name: Create the project directory
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: /opt/dev_projects
        state: directory
        owner: devuser
        group: devuser
        mode: '0775'

    - name: Set permissions for dev_projects to allow group write
      ansible.builtin.command: chmod g+s /opt/dev_projects # Setgid bit for new files to inherit group

Checklist

  • Ensure inventory lists target_servers with correct ansible_user.
  • Run ansible-playbook with --check to preview changes.
  • Verify post-run with id devuser and ls -ld /opt/dev_projects.
Key Takeaway

Use idempotent modules for user and file management, test with dry runs, and validate results on the managed node.

screens.title: Common mistakes, safety checks, and testing
screens.narratorSegment: When adopting Ansible, a few frequent mistakes are worth watching for. Inventory issues often stem from formatting errors or incorrect connection variables; always test groups with the ping module. SSH problems are another common failure: missing keys, wrong ansible_user, or blocked ports will prevent module execution. Module misuse—especially substituting shell for an appropriate module—creates non-idempotent tasks that behave unpredictably on reruns. Privilege escalation mistakes, like forgetting become for package installs, cause task failures that are easy to miss in bulk runs. To mitigate these risks, use ansible-playbook --syntax-check to validate YAML and --check to perform a dry run. Also adopt smaller, frequent changes and version your playbooks and inventories so you can roll back. A misconception is believing --check is a perfect simulation; some modules cannot fully simulate effects, so consider staging runs on a representative environment. Final practice: add a quick syntax-check and dry-run to your workflow before deploying a playbook to production. In practical terms, avoid inventory errors, ssh issues, and non-idempotent tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we build a practical foundation for using Ansible to automate configuration across many servers. You will learn the core architecture — control node, managed nodes, and the inventory — and how Ansible’s agentless model uses SSH to keep setup simple and secure. We will walk through ad-hoc commands for quick checks, then develop a simple playbook that installs and manages Nginx, showing conditionals for different Linux families. You’ll see how modules and tasks produce idempotent changes, why that matters in production, and common mistakes to avoid when configuring inventories and privilege escalation. Finally, you will get a short hands-on lab to create a user and a shared project directory, reinforcing the workflow from inventory to playbook execution. By the end you should be able to run simple ad-hoc commands, author basic playbooks, and reason about when to test versus apply changes in a live environment. Consider how automation reduces manual error and think about which repetitive tasks you would automate first.

These four objectives map to tangible skills you will practice. First, you will explain Ansible’s core concepts and architecture so you can reason about why agentless SSH is both simple and secure; understanding this avoids the common trap of assuming an agent is required. Second, you will set up a control node and configure managed nodes for reliable communication, including SSH key setup and inventory placement. Third, you will run ad-hoc commands to perform immediate checks and fixes; this helps you validate connectivity and run quick diagnostics without writing a playbook. Fourth, you will author simple playbooks to perform repeatable configuration tasks, like installing packages and managing services, and use become and when conditionals to keep tasks safe across distributions. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint to help remember the workflow from inventory to execution. These objectives are intentionally hands-on so you practice both quick commands and structured, reusable automation.

These additional objectives focus on practical application and safety. You will learn to validate and troubleshoot inventories and SSH connectivity so that automation runs reliably. You will practice writing idempotent tasks and using modules appropriately so reruns do not cause unintended changes. You will also learn strategies for testing playbooks, including syntax checks and dry runs, so that changes can be validated before applying to production. Finally, you will learn to use become and understand when privilege escalation is necessary, avoiding common security mistakes such as leaving SSH agents or credentials exposed. Each objective maps to an action: test connectivity, test playbooks, review privilege settings, and run controlled deployments. These behaviours help ensure your automation is safe, reproducible, and maintainable. Learning Objectives — Continued means validate connectivity, write idempotent tasks, test playbooks with --check and --syntax-check, and use become responsibly for safe automation.. In practical terms, skills and behaviours you'll practice in labs and checks. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Configuration Management exists because hand-editing dozens of machines is error-prone and slow. When each host drifts from the documented state, debugging grows harder and outages become likely. Ansible addresses that by letting you express desired state and apply it consistently. A core claim is that automation should be readable, version-controlled, and repeatable. Ansible’s strengths are its agentless architecture and its module library. Being agentless means targets need only standard SSH and, usually, Python. That reduces deployment overhead and easing security reviews. Idempotence is another key idea: modules should make the same change only once and leave the system in the desired state on subsequent runs. For example, using the apt module with state: present installs a package only if it’s missing; running the same task again will not reinstall. A common misconception is that automation removes human oversight; in reality, it shifts your role to designing correct state and tests. To practice, pick one repetitive task you perform today and imagine expressing it as an idempotent Ansible task. What would you need to check first? Why Configuration Management matters and Ansible’s role means configuration management expresses desired state so systems converge predictably and repeatedly; ansible implements this with agentless ssh and idempotent modules.. In practical terms, managing state, reducing error, and scaling changes reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding Ansible architecture helps you design where automation runs and how credentials are managed. The control node is the machine that runs ansible or ansible-playbook; it needs Python and the Ansible package. Managed nodes are the hosts listed in your inventory and do not require an agent because Ansible connects over SSH. When you execute a play, Ansible pushes a small module payload to the managed node and runs it remotely. That module performs the requested operation and returns structured results. This flow means SSH connectivity, key management, and host reachability are critical dependencies. A concrete example: running ansible webservers -m ping from the control node opens SSH connections to each host in the webservers group and executes a small python-based ping module that returns success or failure. A common misconception is that modules remain installed on managed nodes; they are transferred temporarily and removed after execution. Key takeaway: secure SSH keys and verify inventory reachability before automating large runs. How would you validate reachability in your environment? Ansible architecture: Control node, managed nodes, and SSH means control node runs playbooks and pushes temporary modules over ssh to managed nodes, which execute and return results—no persistent agent required.. In practical terms, how communication and execution flow in an agentless model. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An inventory is simply a list of managed nodes organized into groups. The simplest inventory is an INI-style file, often at /etc/ansible/hosts or a custom file you pass with -i. Groups let you target logical sets like webservers or databases. You can also assign variables per-host or per-group to control behavior. For example, adding web1. example. com ansible_user=devops next to a host sets a connection user for that host. Dynamic inventories are scripts or plugins that pull hosts from cloud providers; they are useful when hosts change frequently. A practical example: create a hosts file with a webservers group and a databases group, then run ansible webservers -m ping to verify reachability. Common mistakes include malformed INI syntax or forgetting to expose SSH keys for the user specified in ansible_user. When building inventories, keep them simple and test group targets with the ping module before running playbooks. Which groups would you create for your own infrastructure and why? Inventory basics: groups, host vars, and formats means inventories group hosts and can define per-host or per-group variables; always test groups and connection variables before running playbooks.. In practical terms, organize hosts so plays target the correct machines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Modules are the building blocks of Ansible tasks. Each module encapsulates a specific administrative action — install a package, manage a service, copy a file, or manage users. A crucial property of good modules is idempotence: executing the module multiple times should leave the system in the same state as running it once. Consider the apt module with state: present. If a package is already installed, the module should report no change and not reinstall. This behavior is what lets you run playbooks repeatedly for drift correction without fear of repeated side effects. Modules are executed remotely: Ansible copies the module to the managed node, runs it, and interprets the result. A common mistake is using the shell module for tasks that have a native module; shell commands are often non-idempotent and harder to test. For example, prefer ansible. builtin. user to create a system user rather than a shell adduser sequence. As a practice, review tasks and ask: is there a module that does this idempotently? Ad-hoc commands are one-off Ansible invocations used for quick diagnostics or immediate fixes without creating a playbook. They are useful for validation steps like connectivity checks or fast changes when a scripted playbook would be overkill. A typical example is ansible all -m ping which runs the ping module across every host in the inventory and returns success or failure. Another common ad-hoc usage is ansible webservers -a "uptime" which runs a simple command using the default command module. For package operations you can call a module directly: ansible databases -m apt -a "name=postgresql state=present" to ensure a package is installed on a database group. Remember that ad-hoc commands are powerful but not version-controlled; for repeatable configurations prefer playbooks. A common pitfall is using ad-hoc commands for complex sequences; if you need repeatability or testing, convert the sequence to a playbook. Setting up a control node and managed nodes is a deliberate sequence of steps. First, install Ansible on your control node using your distribution package manager. On Debian: update and apt install ansible; on RHEL-family use dnf or yum. Second, generate SSH keys on the control node with ssh-keygen and copy the public key to managed nodes using ssh-copy-id or manual authorized_keys editing. This enables passwordless authentication, which Ansible prefers. Third, create an inventory file named hosts or my_inventory and add your target hosts into logical groups. Optionally set ansible_user per host if different from your control node account. Fourth, test connectivity with ansible all -m ping or ansible -m ping to confirm reachability. A common mistake is forgetting to configure Python on older minimal images; ensure Python is present as many modules rely on it. Finally, version your inventory and any connection variables in your automation repository so others can reproduce your setup. After these steps you can run ad-hoc commands and playbooks safely. When adopting Ansible, a few frequent mistakes are worth watching for. Inventory issues often stem from formatting errors or incorrect connection variables; always test groups with the ping module. SSH problems are another common failure: missing keys, wrong ansible_user, or blocked ports will prevent module execution. Module misuse—especially substituting shell for an appropriate module—creates non-idempotent tasks that behave unpredictably on reruns. Privilege escalation mistakes, like forgetting become for package installs, cause task failures that are easy to miss in bulk runs. To mitigate these risks, use ansible-playbook --syntax-check to validate YAML and --check to perform a dry run. Also adopt smaller, frequent changes and version your playbooks and inventories so you can roll back. A misconception is believing --check is a perfect simulation; some modules cannot fully simulate effects, so consider staging runs on a representative environment. Final practice: add a quick syntax-check and dry-run to your workflow before deploying a playbook to production. Here are the essential concepts to retain. First, Ansible is agentless: it uses SSH to run temporary modules on managed nodes, reducing setup overhead. Second, the inventory groups hosts and can include variables; always test group reachability before running large plays. Third, modules are idempotent whenever possible, allowing safe reruns without unintended effects.
